extracted.intended_audience: think tank staff — communications leads, researchers, executive directors and events/media officers at policy research centres
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance listing communication channels and tools available to think tanks, with for each: main audience, recommended language/style, typical formats/lengths, and who should manage quality. Includes cross-cutting selection questions and operational notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop strategy for the think tank (not just project)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a communications strategy for the centre and communicate project findings through it — use the centre’s branding, choice of channels and tools, and incorporate project findings into the centre’s broader work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting project-level strategies (often managed by external consultancies) drive communication; instead embed outputs within the centre's identity and longer-term agenda so communications are cumulative and coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate mix of tools and channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all tools fit all centres or projects; each organisation must choose the most appropriate mix of channels and tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guiding questions: Do you have resources and skills? Are main audiences reached? Is there balance between original content and repackaging? How will you keep issues on the public agenda longer? Are tools linked and supporting each other or used in isolation?

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of communication tool complexity (1=basic; 5=elaborate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools are ranked 1 (basic) to 5 (elaborate) to reflect relative complexity/resources required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Levels do not imply chronological progression or minimum centre size. They indicate feasibility (e.g., don't set up an event series if you can't run a single event reliably).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications leader / online communications manager responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A communications lead/specialist should manage most online and outreach tools and be responsible for quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific duties cited across tools: manage website, blog, social accounts, newsletters, events, video/podcast quality decisions, and ensure content is 'Okayed' where needed. Staff may contribute but central oversight is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review and sign-off expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different outputs require different levels of review: internal sign-off by line managers/senior management and external peer review where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: journal articles require external peer review and journal panels; working papers peer reviewed by at least one external reviewer assigned by line manager; research reports peer reviewed by line manager and optionally external reviewer; policy briefs reviewed by senior management and possibly target audience inputs; project briefings need senior management sign-off; opinions and blog posts usually 'Okayed' by line managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop simple audiovisual/copyright policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Centres should create a simple policy on taking and using audio-visual material to ensure respect for copyright and subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should govern use of staff photos, event recordings, third-party images, and permissions; quality expectations should balance production value and accessibility for target audiences and bandwidth constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic journal / journal article standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal or journal article presents final research results aimed at academic/expert communities and should use appropriate academic language and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require external peer review panels (journal-level) and reviewer processes for staff submissions; senior researchers and external reviewers to review staff submissions. Length/style vary by journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic paper (shorter academic output)
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic paper presents research results for academic audiences and should use the expected expert language and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length noted earlier as 2-3 (in ranking); apply usual academic conventions and peer review expectations depending on outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-academic magazine standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Semi-academic magazine presents expert opinion and analysis on public-interest issues in accessible format for a general but informed public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language should be engaging, not shy of technical terms; style should consider modern magazine design; may be fully online; requires a separate management team to commission/edit — typically overseen by communications leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working paper series requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Working papers present preliminary results inviting discussion; aimed at researchers/technical experts and assume subject-matter understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical length: 10,000–40,000 words; use text boxes and graphics; should be peer reviewed by at least one external reviewer assigned by the author’s line manager or project leader if the author is non-staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research report standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A research report is the final report of a research project and is not aimed at a single audience; tone and style vary by case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length: 5,000–30,000 words; include text boxes, graphics, images; peer review by line manager/project leader and external reviewer if senior management deems necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background note (policy/methodology) standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Background notes summarise current knowledge on a policy or research issue (or methods) and suggest future work/implications; not definitive, more accessible than working papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length: ~4–12 pages; include text boxes, graphics, and a relevant cover image; peer reviewed internally unless the centre lacks expertise, in which case include external reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project briefing format and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Project briefings combine background note and research report focusing on a project; aimed at general audiences, especially potential funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length: ~2,500 words; include text boxes, graphics and a cover image; do not require peer review but must be signed off by senior management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy brief purpose and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy briefs provide actionable recommendations to specific policy audiences, drawing from research and other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length: ~2–4 pages; include text boxes, graphics and cover image; write taking into account target audience's knowledge, organisational culture, policy entry points and policy cycle stage; peer reviewed by senior management and possibly include target audience input; sign-off by senior management required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft legislation/regulation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft legislation/regulation offers ready-made policy instruments for policymakers and requires expert knowledge of policymaking systems and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in the language/style demanded by the relevant institution; peer review by senior management and external reviewers with policymaking expertise; develop proposals in consultation with interested/expert parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion piece standards
rubrics_metrics.description: An opinion presents a researcher's personal views on a current policy/research issue aimed at a broad audience; tone accessible, strong and informal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length: no more than 1 page; no references required but include hyperlinks if online; include an author head-shot; should be 'Okayed' by line managers; can be blog form or op-ed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop or event report format
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarises proceedings and key messages from speakers and participants; records names/affiliations only when Chatham House Rule is not invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length: 1–10 pages (longer could be a project briefing or research report); should link to event materials (videos, presentations); should be 'Okayed' by event staff in charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading list / annotated bibliography / literature review guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading lists outline key materials (with links) for interested readers; annotated bibliographies expand with summaries; literature reviews may be intermediary outputs treated as working papers or research reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading lists can be a page on the blog accompanying research projects and should be organised by topics or frameworks where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emailed newsletter best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsletters announce centre activities and direct readers to further materials; they should be short, accessible, and informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All info should be in the body (never attachments); consider basic HTML only; send at appropriate times (e.g., morning before work or before lunch; avoid mid-morning or late afternoon); short content suggests increasing frequency rather than length; managed by communications leader; content need not be reviewed if already 'Okayed'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation's website role and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Website provides information about the organisation and aggregates other communications; should emphasise centre's main arguments rather than just activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make frequent updates, user-friendly navigation, write for the web differently from other formats, use existing technologies rather than bespoke platforms, plan daily/weekly updates for front page; manage by communications leader/online manager; SEO and linking to other tools important; content should already be 'Okayed'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blog use and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Blog announces and introduces new research outputs and events, publishes opinions, reading lists, and highlights multimedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim at a broad audience including other bloggers and opinion-makers; language should be accessible, informal and bold; posts approx. one page, include hyperlinks and multimedia; link blog to website, Facebook, Twitter; communications leader or online manager should manage and edit; staff can post with prior editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitter account practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter accounts announce publications/events, filter information, and encourage discussion; should link to other tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Twitter best practices: short, direct, include links, use hashtags, mention users; managed by communications leader/online manager with staff engagement encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facebook page guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook offers informal engagement for a general audience and can feature recent publications and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Facebook 'rules' and norms; managed by communications leader/online manager with staff engagement encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: LinkedIn for staff profiles and recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff LinkedIn profiles provide up-to-date staff information for the 'about us' page and reduce burden of keeping CVs updated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility lies with individual staff members but profiles should be reviewed by the communications leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube / Ustream for videos and webstreaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Video channels store and share videos and MOOCs, can summarise findings or capture events live; webstreaming requires extra planning to be engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target broad audiences including researchers, policymakers, journalists and donors; style depends on objective (MOOCs pedagogical, talking heads short, animations for complex explanations); quality control by communications leader and researchers; develop audiovisual policy for copyright and subjects; prioritize storyline/content over production value; HD may be inaccessible in some contexts — smartphone/webcam often adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flickr / Picasa image use
rubrics_metrics.description: Images help publications, website design and blog posts; centres can build portfolios using staff pictures or Creative Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a public folder of images for staff headshots, trip photos, event pictures; follow audiovisual/copyright policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: iTunes / podcasts guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Podcasts present information in audio form and often accompany written publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target broad audience and radio stations; language must be clear without visuals; podcasts should be short (no longer than 3 minutes; 30s–1min versions acceptable); should accompany a publication; quality control by communications leader; balance quality and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scribd (document hosting) use
rubrics_metrics.description: Scribd allows uploading publications in shareable formats as an alternative to hosting on own servers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan how to use service (embed vs link); useful for new organisations; consider linking in emails or embedding on pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Google Drive / Dropbox for intranet and sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cloud file-sharing tools can substitute for intranet to organise and share documents among staff and collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisational accounts can be used by researchers; Google Drive also allows making resources public for audiences similar to Scribd.

rubrics_metrics.name: SurveyMonkey for research and outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Online survey tools provide ready-made forms and basic data analysis for research centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider an organisational account for use by individual researchers; useful for polling audiences or collecting data for projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eventbrite for event management
rubrics_metrics.description: Event management tools help manage invites, attendance and dissemination of event information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freed staff to focus on logistics and materials; embed or link events on website/blog and share via social media to widen participation and remote attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wikipedia engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Wikipedia is a top search result and a global knowledge repository; centres should contribute appropriate research references to relevant pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should update pages; communications leader should encourage and help monitor changes to ensure references point back to centre outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data visualisation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Data visualisation tools communicate large datasets to broad or targeted audiences; should focus on a single issue or indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use maps, word clouds, graphs; may require specialised staff but many DIY tools now accessible (link examples); visualisations should be clear and focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Op-ed (newspaper) standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Op-eds in newspapers allow centres to put forward ideas with little editorial interference and reach a wide audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a broad yet relatively informed audience; pieces tend to be short and punchy; neutrality may not be an option; best written by researchers or executive directors with support from communications leader; expect editorial edits by the publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release formatting and targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases inform media about newsworthy projects, outputs or events and must respond to media needs (format, recipients, timing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use centre branding but follow media formatting conventions; start with the news then provide background; send to right contacts at the right time; prepared/managed by communications leader or media officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Q&As
rubrics_metrics.description: Q&As pre-empt journalists' questions or fill knowledge gaps; can be posted online, added to press releases or handed out at events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted at journalists but usable by the public; be very clear, use as many questions as needed; language informal and accessible; developed by communications leader with researchers (possibly via interviews); consider filming audio/video versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media awards as engagement tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Media awards generate interest in policy issues and incentivise journalistic engagement and skill development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards targeted at media but with public impact; can be monetary/non-monetary or research funding; consider partnerships to manage awards; ideally focused on specific policy issues; managed by communications leader/media officer and a researcher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media training for researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Media training helps researchers explain policy and research to journalists and equips journalists with tools to produce accurate stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target various types of journalists; combine lectures with practical story development tied to centre research; managed by communications leader or media officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media partnerships / subcontracts for features and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Partnerships with media organisations enable substantive centre involvement in content development and bespoke products for media outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May involve bespoke reports, data visualisations, indexes, surveys; managed by communications leader in collaboration with executive director and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media face-to-face briefings
rubrics_metrics.description: Face-to-face briefings with editors or specialised journalists provide candid, often off-the-record conversations to strengthen mutual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended as listening as much as talking; organise by communications leaders/media officers to build media relationships; be candid but aware there is no absolute off-the-record guarantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshops and trainings design and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops/trainings present findings and facilitate discussion and practice; they support capacity development and application of methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target interested participants and tailor language to their level; combine professional facilitation, practical exercises, and researcher involvement; link with other outputs for follow-up; developed/managed by researchers with support of communications/events manager.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seminar presentation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Seminars allow presenting new ideas to informed audiences; more effective when researchers present an opinion elaborating on findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume audience knowledge level; language must be engaging; presenters should use modern presentation tools and multimedia (avoid word-heavy PowerPoints); developed by researchers with communications support for style consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Webinar planning considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Webinars present workshop/seminar content using online tools to include remote participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should account for internet access constraints; plan interactive elements suitable for remote engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public events (debates and presentations) best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Public events present ideas or research to informed interested audiences and must consider panel composition and event structure for impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose credible speakers; structure events for impact (invitations well in advance, 1–2 hour length, schedule at appropriate times, include different views, provide supporting materials, allow Q&A, record proceedings); managed by communications leader/events manager in close collaboration with researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public event series advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Event series sustain an issue on the agenda longer and can attract sponsorship and broader engagement; should be prioritised over one-off events where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan series strategically to build a body of knowledge and longer-term visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private meetings with key stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Private meetings present the organisation, argue solutions, or maintain relationships; messages must be tailored to specific audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct stakeholder analysis (e.g., Alignment/Interest/Influence Matrix) beforehand; avoid perceptions of unethical lobbying; consider leaving materials behind; executive director closely involved but researchers and communications leader can organise; establish back-to-office reports to capture learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: MOOC pedagogical and management guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: MOOCs present research methods/theory/findings for educational purposes and reach global audiences; style can be academic but should combine multimedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience registration can help define participant knowledge; may be short stand-alone or series of videos; management may fall to communications leader or researchers; seek pedagogical quality assurance; hosting via third-party platforms includes platform-specific conditions.
